claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Kimura et al., 2013) documenting failed antibody responses in patients with elevated MDSC.

claims.claim: Adoptive transfer of activated L-selectin+CCR7+ stem cell memory T cells (TSCM) has greater antitumor efficacy than terminally differentiated L-selectinloCCR7lo cytolytic effectors.

claims.source: The superior efficacy of TSCM is attributed to the requirement for adoptively-transferred cells to undergo L-selectin-dependent trafficking via HEV to access intranodal growth and survival factors (Gattinoni et al., 2005).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Gattinoni et al., 2005) explaining mechanism of TSCM efficacy.

claims.claim: The efficacy of ACT therapy is limited by MDSC.

claims.claim: An unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that an unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo two major MDSC-mediated events that impair T cell responses in LN: (1) reduced LN homing due to rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr, and (2) immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing rapid L-selectin loss on transferred T cells in MDSC-rich environment.

claims.claim: An unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
claims.source: Our findings suggest that an unexpected outcome of clinical ACT immunotherapy in patients with high MDSC burdens is that a high proportion of transferred T cells will undergo two major MDSC-mediated events that impair T cell responses in LN: (1) reduced LN homing due to rapid L-selectin loss within 24 hr, and (2) immune suppression stemming from T cell preconditioning prior to direct tumor-antigen exposure.
claims.evidence: Inference based on experimental data showing MDSC preconditioning reduces T cell responsiveness to antigen.

claims.claim: These MDSC-mediated mechanisms would necessitate the transfer of excessive numbers of ex vivo-expanded T cells to achieve therapeutic efficacy in ACT therapy.
claims.source: These mechanisms would necessitate the transfer of excessive numbers of ex vivo-expanded T cells to achieve therapeutic efficacy.
claims.evidence: Inference based on observed MDSC-mediated impairment of transferred T cell function.

claims.claim: L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells.
claims.source: Findings that L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells suggest that neoadjuvant treatments that target MDSC could offer promise for immune-based cancer therapies that depend on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.

claims.claim: Neoadjuvant treatments that target MDSC could offer promise for immune-based cancer therapies that depend on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.

claims.evidence: Inference based on reversibility of L-selectin loss after MDSC removal.

claims.claim: Tumor-induced MDSC act from remote sites through two independent mechanisms to suppress systemic adaptive immunity in widely dispersed LN.

claims.evidence: Summary claim based on multiple experimental findings throughout the study.

claims.claim: Moderate L-selectin loss causes a profound reduction in antigen-driven expansion of CD8+ T cells within the LN stroma.

claims.evidence: Supported by competitive activation assay data in Figure 8 showing ~70:1 ratio of activated L-selectinhi vs L-selectinint/lo OT-I cells in draining LN.

claims.claim: MDSC-induced L-selectin down-modulation could compromise immunotherapy regimens dependent on immune cell access to LN.

claims.claim: The spleen is a major reservoir for peripheral MDSC with direct immunosuppressive activity.

claims.claim: The blood is not known to be an active site of MDSC function in situ.

claims.claim: The blood is a major site for MDSC-targeted L-selectin downregulation for both T and B cells.

claims.claim: MDSC-to-target cell contact is a prerequisite for L-selectin down-modulation.

claims.evidence: Supported by transwell co-culture experiments in Figure 4D showing contact-dependence.

claims.claim: Biological consequences occur as a result of cell-to-cell interactions within the blood.

claims.evidence: General statement about precedent in other biological systems used to support plausibility of MDSC function in blood.

claims.claim: Leukocyte-leukocyte interactions along vessel walls contribute to recruitment at inflammatory sites.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Krebs et al., 2014) documenting traveling niches in metastasis.

claims.claim: Naïve lymphocytes are transiently retained in intravascular niches in the lung.

claims.claim: L-selectin status is a critical determinant of homing potential since lymphocytes emigrating from spleen or blood have nearly immediate access to LN HEV.

claims.evidence: Inference based on lymphocyte recirculation patterns, supported by citation to prior literature (Chen et al., 2006).

claims.claim: The extent of the homing defect in HEV is remarkable considering the modest change in overall L-selectin surface density observed for T cells in the AT-3 tumor model.

claims.evidence: Interpretation of experimental findings comparing magnitude of L-selectin loss to magnitude of homing defect.

claims.claim: During leukocyte rolling it is estimated that ~5 microvillous tips are in simultaneous contact with endothelial surfaces, with L-selectin concentration exceeding 90,000 molecules per μm2 at a single microvillous tip.
claims.source: During leukocyte rolling it is estimated that ~5 microvillous tips are in simultaneous contact with endothelial surfaces, with L-selectin concentration exceeding 90,000 molecules per μm2 at a single microvillous tip (Shao and Hochmuth, 1999).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Shao and Hochmuth, 1999) documenting L-selectin distribution during rolling.

claims.claim: Relatively subtle decreases in L-selectin density within multivalent focal patches increase rolling speed, thus destabilizing adhesion within HEV.

claims.claim: Intermediate L-selectin downregulation in genetically engineered L-selectin+/− T cells causes diminished rolling quality.

claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Tang et al., 1998; Gauguet et al., 2004) documenting rolling defects in L-selectin+/− cells.

claims.claim: L-selectin modulation by MDSC is of primary importance during adhesion on the lumenal surface of HEV prior to extravasation.

claims.claim: MDSC-mediated L-selectin loss may have downstream consequences in controlling the polarity of monocytes necessary for transendothelial migration.

claims.evidence: Supported by citation to prior literature (Yang et al., 2011) documenting L-selectin role in CD8+ T cell function.

claims.claim: There is an unprecedented correlation between MDSC expansion, L-selectin loss by T and B lymphocytes, and a >2 fold increase in circulating sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice.

claims.evidence: Supported by ELISA data in Figure 5B showing elevated serum sL-selectin in 4T1-bearing mice.

claims.claim: Serum sL-selectin levels are increased in patients with solid tumors (bladder and thyroid cancer).

claims.evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature (Choudhary et al., 2015; Kobawala et al., 2016) documenting elevated sL-selectin in cancer patients.

claims.claim: Partial MDSC depletion (~50%) by administration of anti-Gr-1 antibody at three day intervals after 4T1 implantation had no impact on tumor growth but significantly rescued L-selectin on circulating naïve T and B cells.

claims.claim: Two independent but complementary mechanisms are proposed to reduce LN trafficking in cancer: (1) MDSC-directed downregulation of lymphocyte L-selectin which negatively impacts homing in HEV, and (2) elevated circulating sL-selectin which functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo.

results.result: MDSC are absent from thymus and lymph nodes (LN) in 4T1 tumor-bearing mice, with no L-selectin modulation on naïve T cells in these compartments. MDSC exclusion from LN is attributed to their low L-selectin expression, and the uniformly high L-selectin on intranodal T cells suggests a stringent requirement for L-selectin-mediated entry across HEV.
results.evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are well-supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing absence of CD11b+Gr-1+ cells in thymus and LN, maintained L-selectin expression on T cells in these compartments, and lower L-selectin on MDSC compared to naïve T cells. The inference about L-selectin threshold for HEV entry (C6) is reasonable given the consistent observation of high L-selectin on intranodal T cells.

results.result: Profound L-selectin downregulation occurs on naïve CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in blood and spleen of 4T1-bearing mice, correlating with substantial MDSC elevation. Splenic CD11b+Gr-1+ cells exhibit prototypical MDSC suppressor function in vitro. Naïve T cells decrease in LN and increase in spleen without changes in apoptosis, supporting compensatory redistribution due to reduced L-selectin-dependent LN access.
results.evaluation: Claims C7-C11 are supported by flow cytometric data in Figure 1A showing L-selectin downregulation and MDSC accumulation in blood/spleen, T cell suppression assays in Figure 1B demonstrating MDSC function, and cell quantification in Figure 1C showing redistribution without increased apoptosis. The inference about compensatory redistribution (C11) is reasonable given the observed changes in T cell distribution.

results.result: L-selectin loss on splenic T cells correlates temporally with MDSC expansion across different murine tumor models. In 4T1 tumors, L-selectin downregulation occurs early (day 7) and increases with tumor burden. AT-3 tumors show delayed MDSC expansion and moderate L-selectin loss at ≥21 days. B16 and CT26 tumors show L-selectin downregulation only in rare mice with abundant MDSC, consistent with these tumors not typically inducing MDSC expansion.
results.evaluation: Claims C12-C18 are supported by longitudinal flow cytometric data in Figure 1—figure supplements 2-4 showing temporal correlation between MDSC accumulation and L-selectin downregulation across multiple tumor models. Citations to prior literature (C18) appropriately document MDSC expansion patterns in B16 and CT26 models. The data demonstrate model-dependent kinetics of MDSC expansion and L-selectin loss.

results.result: Immunohistological analysis reveals spatial segregation in spleen: Gr-1+ MDSC congregate with CD3+ T cells in the marginal zone but are excluded from B220+ B cell follicles. Splenic B cells express lower L-selectin than T cells, and L-selectin density on B cells is unchanged in tumor-bearing mice. This differential regulation suggests close physical contact with MDSC is required for L-selectin loss.
results.evaluation: Claims C19-C22 are supported by immunofluorescence data in Figure 1D showing spatial distribution of MDSC, T cells, and B cells, and flow cytometric data in Figure 1E showing maintained L-selectin on B cells despite downregulation on T cells. The inference about contact-dependence (C22) is reasonable given the spatial correlation between MDSC localization and L-selectin loss. Citations to prior literature (C20) appropriately document baseline B cell L-selectin expression.

results.result: Splenectomy experiments demonstrate that L-selectin downregulation on adoptively transferred CD8+ T cells occurs independently of the splenic microenvironment. Tumor growth and blood MDSC levels are equivalent in sham and splenectomized 4T1-bearing mice. L-selectin is maintained on transferred T cells in non-tumor bearing recipients but lost within 24 hr in tumor-bearing recipients regardless of splenectomy status, indicating L-selectin down-modulation can occur in the intravascular space.
results.evaluation: Claims C23-C29 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 2B-C showing equivalent tumor growth and MDSC burden in sham vs. splenectomized mice, and similar L-selectin downregulation on transferred T cells in both groups. The conclusion that L-selectin loss can occur in blood (C29) is a reasonable inference from these splenectomy experiments. Citations to prior work on splenectomy effects in lung tumor models (C25) provide appropriate context.

results.result: L-selectin is strongly downregulated on endogenous CD4+ T cells in tumor-bearing mice regardless of splenectomy. For B cells, L-selectin is maintained in bone marrow and spleen but nearly completely downregulated in blood of both sham and splenectomized tumor-bearing mice, identifying blood as the preferential site of B cell L-selectin modulation. This occurs rapidly (2 hr post-adoptive transfer), before lymphocytes can recirculate through tissues (transit times: T cells 5-24 hr, B cells ~24 hr).
results.evaluation: Claims C30-C39 are supported by flow cytometric data in Figures 2—figure supplement 1 and Figure 3 showing tissue-specific L-selectin regulation on T and B cells, and Figure 3—figure supplement 2 showing rapid (2 hr) L-selectin loss post-transfer. Citations to prior literature (C31, C37-C39) appropriately document B cell L-selectin regulation and lymphocyte transit times. The inference about blood as the preferential site (C34) is well-supported by the compartment-specific data.

results.result: Lymphocytes are the primary source of circulating soluble L-selectin (sL-selectin) under normal conditions (~70% reduction in Rag2−/− mice). Increased serum sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice (1 µg/mL vs. ~0.4 µg/mL in controls) likely reflects MDSC-induced cleavage from lymphocyte membranes. At these concentrations, sL-selectin reportedly functions as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed lymphocyte homing in vivo (40-65% reduction at 0.9-1.5 µg/mL; no inhibition at ~0.6 µg/mL).
results.evaluation: Claims C40-C45 are supported by citations to prior literature documenting sL-selectin sources (C40-C41) and dose-dependent homing inhibition (C44-C45). The inference about MDSC-induced cleavage (C42) is reasonable given the correlation between MDSC expansion, lymphocyte L-selectin loss, and elevated sL-selectin. The proposed dual mechanism of L-selectin downregulation and elevated sL-selectin (C43) is a logical synthesis of the data, though direct functional evidence for sL-selectin antagonism in this system is not provided.

results.result: MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation does not depend on ADAM17 acting in cis or trans. MDSC do not activate lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 (shown using Adam17−/− lymphocytes), nor does MDSC-expressed ADAM17 act in trans (shown using ADAM17 inhibitors and L(E)-selectin mutant cells). The mechanism parallels ADAM17/ADAM10-independent ecto-protease activity reported for constitutive/inducible L-selectin shedding. MDSC are enriched for multiple ecto-proteases including MMP3, which can cleave L-selectin in vitro.
results.evaluation: Claims C46-C52 are well-supported by comprehensive experimental data in Figure 5C-E using ADAM17 inhibitors, L(E)-selectin mutant mice, and Adam17−/− mice showing MDSC-induced L-selectin loss is ADAM17-independent. Citations to prior literature appropriately document ADAM17-independent L-selectin shedding mechanisms (C50), MDSC ecto-protease expression (C51), and MMP3-mediated L-selectin cleavage (C52). The conclusion that another ecto-protease is involved is a reasonable inference from the exclusion of ADAM17/ADAM10.

results.result: B cells are targets of tumor-induced MDSC, representing the first demonstration of this relationship. Nearly complete L-selectin loss on circulating B cells strongly suggests B cell homing at HEV would be blocked, given B cell sensitivity to L-selectin perturbations. Antibody responses would be severely diminished due to suboptimal trafficking of both naïve B cells and CD4+ follicular helper T cell precursors. This could explain failed antibody responses to MUC-1 vaccination in patients with elevated MDSC.
results.evaluation: Claims C53-C59 are supported by flow cytometric data showing nearly complete L-selectin loss on blood B cells (Figure 3), citations to prior literature documenting B cell support of MDSC (C53), MDSC suppression of B cells in autoimmunity (C55), B cell sensitivity to L-selectin levels (C57), and failed vaccination responses in MDSC-high patients (C59). The inferences about blocked B cell homing (C56) and diminished antibody responses (C58) are reasonable extrapolations from the data, though direct functional evidence is not provided.

results.result: Adoptive cell transfer (ACT) of L-selectin+CCR7+ stem cell memory T cells (TSCM) has greater antitumor efficacy than terminally differentiated effectors, attributed to L-selectin-dependent trafficking to access intranodal growth factors. ACT efficacy is limited by MDSC. In patients with high MDSC burdens, transferred T cells would undergo rapid L-selectin loss (within 24 hr) and immune suppression from MDSC preconditioning, necessitating transfer of excessive T cell numbers to achieve efficacy.
results.evaluation: Claims C60-C65 are supported by citations to prior literature documenting TSCM efficacy (C60-C61) and MDSC limitation of ACT (C62), combined with experimental data from the current study showing rapid L-selectin loss on transferred T cells (24 hr, Figure 2C) and MDSC preconditioning effects (Figure 8—figure supplement 1). The inferences about clinical ACT outcomes (C63-C65) are reasonable extrapolations from the experimental data, though they represent speculation about human therapy rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: L-selectin loss is not indelibly imprinted on T cells, as shown by complete recovery within four days after MDSC depletion. This reversibility suggests neoadjuvant treatments targeting MDSC could benefit immune-based cancer therapies dependent on T and B cell trafficking to lymph nodes.
results.evaluation: Claims C66-C67 are supported by experimental data in Figure 4C showing L-selectin recovery on T cells after MDSC depletion in vitro and in vivo. The inference about therapeutic potential (C67) is a reasonable speculation based on the reversibility data, though it represents a proposed future direction rather than tested intervention.

results.result: Tumor-induced MDSC act from remote sites (spleen and blood) to suppress systemic adaptive immunity in widely dispersed LN through two independent mechanisms. MDSC downregulate L-selectin on naïve CD4+/CD8+ T cells and blood-borne B cells. Even moderate L-selectin loss severely limits CD8+ T cell trafficking across HEV and causes profound reduction in antigen-driven expansion within LN stroma. This could impair immune surveillance during early tumor escape and compromise immunotherapy regimens dependent on immune cell access to LN.
results.evaluation: Claims C68-C73 represent major summary conclusions supported by the comprehensive experimental data throughout the study: flow cytometry showing L-selectin downregulation (Figures 1-3), intravital microscopy demonstrating trafficking defects (Figure 6), competitive homing assays (Figure 7), and competitive activation assays (Figure 8). The inferences about clinical implications (C72-C73) are reasonable extrapolations from the experimental findings, though they represent speculation about disease progression and therapy rather than direct experimental evidence.

results.result: T cells can be preconditioned by MDSC in spleen or blood, resulting in diminished responsiveness to subsequent antigen challenge. LN are important sites of MDSC suppression despite MDSC exclusion from this compartment, which could not be predicted from routine immune profiling.
results.evaluation: Claims C74-C75 are supported by in vitro preconditioning assays (Figure 8—figure supplement 1) and in vivo competitive activation assays (Figure 8) showing reduced T cell responses after MDSC exposure. The inference about LN as important sites of MDSC suppression (C75) is a reasonable conclusion given the profound impact on intranodal T cell responses despite MDSC exclusion from LN.

results.result: The spleen is a major reservoir for MDSC with immunosuppressive activity, while blood was not previously known as an active site of MDSC function. MDSC are compartmentalized in the splenic marginal zone, linked to T cell but not B cell L-selectin downregulation. Splenectomy experiments reveal blood as a major site for MDSC-targeted L-selectin downregulation. MDSC-to-target cell contact is required for L-selectin down-modulation. High circulating MDSC concentrations (up to 45% of PBMC in cancer patients) make serial contact with lymphocytes plausible in blood, multicellular aggregates, or intravascular niches.
results.evaluation: Claims C76-C87 are supported by citations to prior literature documenting splenic MDSC function (C76), immunofluorescence data showing MDSC compartmentalization (Figure 1D, C78-C79), splenectomy experiments demonstrating blood as a major site of L-selectin loss (Figures 2-3, C80), transwell experiments showing contact-dependence (Figure 4D, C81), and citations documenting cell-cell interactions in blood (C83-C84), MDSC frequencies in patients (C85), and lymphocyte retention in lung (C86). The statement about blood not being known as an active MDSC site (C77) appropriately characterizes prior knowledge.

results.result: The extent of the homing defect in HEV is remarkable considering the modest L-selectin loss in AT-3 tumors. During rolling, ~5 microvillous tips contact endothelial surfaces with L-selectin concentration >90,000 molecules/µm2 per tip. Relatively subtle decreases in L-selectin density within these multivalent focal patches increase rolling speed, destabilizing adhesion in HEV. L-selectin modulation by MDSC is of primary importance during adhesion on the HEV lumenal surface prior to extravasation, though downstream consequences in transendothelial migration and cytolytic function acquisition cannot be excluded.
results.evaluation: Claims C88-C94 are supported by intravital microscopy data showing increased rolling velocity and reduced sticking despite modest L-selectin loss (Figure 6), citations to prior literature documenting L-selectin distribution during rolling (C89) and rolling defects in L-selectin+/− cells (C91), and citations documenting additional L-selectin functions (C93-C94). The interpretation about the importance of L-selectin density in multivalent focal patches (C90) is a reasonable mechanistic inference from the rolling velocity data.

results.result: There is an unprecedented correlation between MDSC expansion, L-selectin loss by T and B lymphocytes, and >2-fold increase in circulating sL-selectin in tumor-bearing mice. Serum sL-selectin levels are also increased in patients with solid tumors (bladder and thyroid cancer), though links to MDSC were not explored in those studies.
results.evaluation: Claims C95-C96 are supported by ELISA data in Figure 5B showing elevated serum sL-selectin in 4T1-bearing mice, and citations to clinical studies documenting elevated sL-selectin in cancer patients (C96). The characterization as "unprecedented" (C95) is appropriate given the novel demonstration of the three-way correlation in this study.

results.result: Partial MDSC depletion (~50%) by anti-Gr-1 antibody significantly rescues L-selectin on circulating T and B cells without affecting tumor growth. L-selectin loss is reversible: complete recovery occurs within four days after MDSC depletion from L-selectinlo splenic populations, demonstrating continued MDSC exposure is required to maintain L-selectin down-modulation. In vitro, MDSC cause stronger L-selectin loss when IFN-γ and LPS are included to sustain MDSC function, and act through a contact-dependent mechanism abrogated by transwell separation.
results.evaluation: Claims C97-C103 are well-supported by experimental data in Figure 4A-D showing L-selectin rescue after anti-Gr-1 treatment, L-selectin recovery after MDSC depletion in vitro and in vivo, enhanced L-selectin loss with IFN-γ/LPS, and contact-dependence demonstrated by transwell experiments. Citations to prior literature (C101) appropriately document IFN-γ/LPS effects on MDSC function. The conclusion that MDSC directly target lymphocytes (C103) is well-supported by the multiple experimental approaches.

results.result: L-selectin mRNA levels are unchanged in splenic T cells of 4T1-bearing mice, indicating L-selectin loss does not involve transcriptional repression. Instead, MDSC-mediated L-selectin downmodulation is accompanied by 2.5-fold increase in serum sL-selectin, consistent with a sheddase-dependent mechanism. L-selectin is a well-known target of the ADAM17 ecto-protease operating in cis.
results.evaluation: Claims C104-C108 are supported by qRT-PCR data in Figure 5A showing unchanged mRNA levels, ELISA data in Figure 5B showing elevated serum sL-selectin, and citation to prior literature documenting ADAM17-mediated L-selectin cleavage (C108). The inference that L-selectin loss does not involve transcriptional repression (C105) is reasonable given unchanged mRNA despite reduced protein. The inference about sheddase-dependent mechanism (C107) is reasonable given elevated sL-selectin.

results.result: PMA-induced L-selectin loss is abrogated by ADAM17-specific inhibitor (PF-5480090), dual ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitor (INCB7839), L(E)-selectin mutation, and ADAM17 deficiency, confirming strict requirement for cis-acting ADAM17. In contrast, MDSC-induced L-selectin downregulation is unaffected by ADAM17/ADAM10 inhibitors, L(E)-selectin mutation, or lymphocyte-intrinsic ADAM17 deficiency in vitro and in vivo. These data exclude a role for ADAM17 or ADAM10 in either cis or trans orientation for MDSC-induced L-selectin loss and suggest involvement of another ecto-protease.
results.evaluation: Claims C109-C120 are comprehensively supported by experimental data in Figure 5C-E using multiple complementary approaches: ADAM17 inhibitors, L(E)-selectin mutant mice, and Adam17−/− mice. The head-to-head comparison between PMA-induced (ADAM17-dependent) and MDSC-induced (ADAM17-independent) L-selectin loss is particularly strong. Citations to prior literature appropriately document ADAM17 requirement for PMA-induced shedding (C113). The conclusion excluding ADAM17/ADAM10 (C119) and suggesting another ecto-protease (C120) are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence.

results.result: L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells from AT-3-bearing mice exhibit normal frequency of tethering and rolling interactions in HEV but show significant decrease in transition from rolling to firm arrest in order IV and V venules, despite normal CCR7 and LFA-1 expression and function. L-selectinint/lo cells exhibit significantly faster median rolling velocity (65.0 vs. 37.2 µm/sec) compared to L-selectinhi cells in order V venular segments.
results.evaluation: Claims C121-C124 are well-supported by intravital microscopy data in Figure 6C-E showing normal rolling fractions but reduced sticking fractions and increased rolling velocities for AT-3 CD8+ T cells, and functional assays in Figure 6—figure supplement 1 showing normal CCR7 and LFA-1 expression and function. The data provide strong evidence that moderate L-selectin loss specifically affects rolling quality and transition to firm arrest without affecting initial tethering/rolling or downstream adhesion molecule function.

results.result: Homeostatic trafficking of L-selectinint/lo CD8+ T cells across LN HEV is strongly inhibited (~80%) compared to L-selectinhi T cells. Transferred CD8+ T cells that successfully extravasate are uniformly L-selectinhi regardless of origin, suggesting high L-selectin density is necessary to stabilize adhesion during extravasation. Differential L-selectin expression is maintained in spleen where trafficking is not L-selectin-dependent. Reduced trafficking due to moderate L-selectin loss also occurs in inflammatory conditions (WBH-treated mice with elevated HEV CCL21 and ICAM-1).
results.evaluation: Claims C125-C130 are well-supported by competitive homing assay data in Figure 7A showing ~80% reduction in LN homing of AT-3 CD8+ T cells, flow cytometric analysis in Figure 7B showing L-selectinhi phenotype on T cells recovered from LN but maintained differential expression in spleen, and immunofluorescence data in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 showing elevated CCL21 and ICAM-1 in WBH-treated mice. The inference about L-selectin density requirement for extravasation (C127) is reasonable given the selective homing of L-selectinhi cells.

results.result: In vitro, OT-I T cells from non-tumor bearing mice are ≥2 times more responsive to antigen-driven proliferation than OT-I cells from AT-3-bearing mice. Transient MDSC co-culture (16 hr preconditioning) followed by MDSC removal markedly suppresses T cell proliferation during subsequent antigen challenge. In vivo, activated L-selectinhi OT-I T cells from tumor-free donors outnumber L-selectinint/lo OT-I cells from AT-3-bearing donors by ~70:1 in draining LN four days post-vaccination, with no bias in contralateral LN or spleen. The profound discrepancy between in vitro (2:1) and in vivo (70:1) ratios supports a model where MDSC operate at distal sites to subvert adaptive immunity by restricting L-selectin-directed access to cognate antigens in LN.
results.evaluation: Claims C131-C136 are well-supported by in vitro competitive activation assays in Figure 8B showing 2:1 bias, preconditioning assays in Figure 8—figure supplement 1 showing suppressed proliferation after MDSC exposure, and in vivo competitive activation assays in Figure 8C showing dramatic 70:1 bias in draining LN but not in contralateral LN or spleen. The comparison between in vitro and in vivo results (C136) provides strong evidence that the trafficking defect amplifies the intrinsic suppression caused by MDSC preconditioning.

results.result: Regional LN are major lines of defense against cancer, serving as hubs for adaptive immunity generation. A rate-limiting step for immune surveillance involves trafficking at HEV to ensure DC present antigens to a diverse T cell repertoire. Two independent but complementary mechanisms are proposed to reduce LN trafficking in cancer: (1) MDSC-directed downregulation of lymphocyte L-selectin negatively impacting HEV homing, and (2) elevated circulating sL-selectin (1 µg/mL in tumor-bearing vs. ~0.4 µg/mL in controls) functioning as a competitive antagonist of L-selectin-directed homing.
results.evaluation: Claims C137-C139 represent summary conclusions synthesizing the major findings. C137-C138 are supported by citations to prior literature documenting LN function in immunity. C139 is supported by the experimental data showing L-selectin downregulation and elevated sL-selectin throughout the study. The proposed dual mechanism model (C139) is a reasonable synthesis of the findings, though direct functional evidence for sL-selectin antagonism at the measured concentrations in this specific system is not provided.
